Tom managed to scratch up the cupboard with it and was getting ready to start on the dresser when he was called away to dress for Sunday school.

Mary handed him a tin bowl of water and a piece of soap. He went outside and placed the bowl on a little bench by the door. Then he dipped the soap in the water, set it down, rolled up his sleeves, and carefully poured the water onto the ground. After that he went into the kitchen and began rubbing his face hard with the towel behind the door. But Mary took the towel away.

“Aren’t you ashamed of yourself, Tom? You mustn’t behave so badly. Water won’t hurt you.”

Tom felt a little embarrassed. The bowl was filled again, and this time he stood over it for a while, working up his courage. He drew a deep breath and began. Soon he came back into the kitchen with both eyes shut, feeling around for the towel. Soap and water dripped from his face as honest proof of his efforts. But when he finished drying, the result still wasn’t good enough. The clean area ended at his chin and jaw like a mask. Below and beyond that line, a dark stretch of unwashed dirt ran down the front and around the back of his neck. Mary took charge. When she finished, he was a fellow human being with no difference in color from one part to another. His soaking hair was neatly brushed, its short curls arranged into a pretty, balanced shape. In private, he worked hard to flatten those curls and plaster his hair against his head. He thought curls were girlish, and his own were a constant source of misery. Mary then brought out the suit he had worn only on Sundays for two years. They called it his “other clothes,” which tells us how large his wardrobe was. After he dressed, she straightened everything: buttoned his tidy short jacket up to his chin, folded his enormous shirt collar down over his shoulders, brushed him off, and topped him with his spotted straw hat. He looked much better and extremely uncomfortable. He felt every bit as uncomfortable as he looked. Being clean and wearing clothes without holes made him feel painfully restricted. He hoped Mary would forget his shoes, but that hope was crushed. She covered them well with tallow, as people usually did, and brought them out. He lost his temper and complained that he was always forced to do everything he didn’t want to do.

Suddenly the painter appeared in the studio doorway and waved them inside with quick, sharp gestures. They looked at each other and smiled.

“I’m waiting,” he called. “Please come in. The light is perfect, and you can bring your drinks.”

They stood and walked slowly down the path together. Two green-and-white butterflies fluttered past. In the pear tree at the corner of the garden, a thrush began to sing.

“You’re glad you met me, Mr. Gray,” Lord Henry said, looking at him.

“Yes, I’m glad now. I wonder whether I always will be.”

“Always! What a dreadful word. Hearing it makes me shudder. Women love using it. They spoil every romance by trying to make it last forever. And the word means nothing. The only difference between a passing fancy and a lifelong passion is that the passing fancy lasts a little longer.”

As they entered the studio, Dorian Gray rested his hand on Lord Henry’s arm. “Then let our friendship be a passing fancy,” he murmured, blushing at his own boldness. He stepped onto the platform and returned to his pose.

Lord Henry dropped into a large wicker armchair and watched him. The brush swept and flicked across the canvas, making the only sound in the quiet, except when Hallward occasionally stepped back to see his work from a distance. Dust danced golden in the slanting sunlight coming through the open door. The heavy fragrance of roses seemed to hang over everything.

About fifteen minutes later, Hallward stopped painting. He looked at Dorian Gray for a long time, then at the portrait for just as long, frowning and biting the end of one of his large brushes. “It’s completely finished,” he announced at last. Bending down, he signed his name in long, bright red letters in the canvas’s left-hand corner.

Lord Henry walked over to inspect the painting. It was certainly a wonderful work of art, and it captured Dorian wonderfully too.

“My dear friend, my warmest congratulations,” he said. “It’s the finest portrait of modern times. Mr. Gray, come and look at yourself.”

The young man gave a start, as though waking from a dream.

“Is it really finished?” he murmured, stepping off the platform.

“Completely,” the painter replied. “And you posed splendidly today. I’m very grateful.”

“You have me entirely to thank for that,” Lord Henry interrupted. “Don’t you agree, Mr. Gray?”

Dorian did not reply. He moved without enthusiasm to stand before his portrait, then turned to look at it.

It now showed my elevation to be 132,000 feet, or twenty-five miles; thus at that moment I surveyed no less than one three-hundred-and-twentieth of the earth’s entire surface. By nine o’clock the land to the east had again vanished from view, though not before I perceived that the balloon was drifting swiftly north-northwest. The curvature of the ocean below was strikingly clear, although drifting banks of cloud repeatedly obscured the prospect. I noticed that even the frailest vapors rose no higher than ten miles above sea level.

“At half past nine I experimented by casting a handful of feathers out through the valve. Rather than floating as I had anticipated, they plunged straight downward together, like a bullet, with tremendous speed, and disappeared within a few seconds. At first I could find no explanation for this remarkable occurrence, since I could not believe my ascent had suddenly accelerated to such an extraordinary degree. Soon, however, it struck me that the air had become too thin to support even feathers. They had indeed fallen rapidly, just as they seemed to, and what astonished me was the combined speed of their descent and my rise.

“By ten I discovered that little required my immediate attention. Everything proceeded admirably, and I believed the balloon was ascending at a speed that increased every moment, though I could no longer measure the rate of that increase. I felt neither pain nor discomfort of any sort, and my spirits were better than at any time since leaving Rotterdam. I occupied myself alternately with inspecting my several instruments and renewing the atmosphere inside the chamber. I resolved to perform this latter task regularly every forty minutes, less because such frequent renewal was strictly necessary than to safeguard my health. Meanwhile I could not resist imagining what lay ahead. My fancy delighted in the moon’s wild, dreamlike regions. Imagination, freed for once from her restraints, wandered wherever she pleased through the shifting marvels of an indistinct and changeable land. At one moment there were ancient, venerable forests, jagged cliffs, and waterfalls crashing noisily into bottomless chasms. At the next I found myself abruptly in hushed noonday wildernesses, where no breath of wind ever entered, and where immense fields of poppies and slender flowers resembling lilies stretched to a weary distance, forever motionless and silent.
